Abstaining when inputs are missing: worst-case bounds, imputation spread and pattern submodels compared for prescreening elevated depressive symptoms in NHANES
Truong Hai Bang, Van An Phan Thi

This file gives the extended methods (Section S1), extended results (Section S2), additional discussion (Section S3), additional tables and figures (Section S4) and the TRIPOD+AI checklist (Section S5). It is the full-length version from which the main text was condensed; references to 'main text' point to the article. References are numbered for this file.
S1. Extended methods
S1.1. Study design, intended use and reporting

This is a retrospective study that develops prediction models and compares rules for abstaining when inputs are missing, reported following TRIPOD+AI [27] (checklist in Section S5). Both validation cohorts come from later or earlier periods of the same survey, so in TRIPOD terms both are temporal validations; we call them later-period (2021–2023) and earlier-period (2005–2014) validation. The intended user is a service or analyst holding survey or record information without symptom items; the intended action is to recommend completing the PHQ-9 or an equivalent assessment. Where a person can be asked two questions, the PHQ-2 is the appropriate first step, and we report it as a reference point (Section S1.11). The models do not diagnose major depressive disorder, do not estimate future incidence and are not tools for assessing self-harm risk. Predictors and outcome are measured in the same survey, so the target is concurrent elevated symptoms. All estimates are unweighted and refer to study participants unless stated otherwise.
S1.2. Data sources

NHANES is a continuous cross-sectional survey of the non-institutionalised United States population. Development data came from the 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic release, which combines the 2017–2018 cycle with data collected until fieldwork was suspended in March 2020 [28]. Later-period validation used August 2021–August 2023, and earlier-period validation the five two-year cycles 2005–2006 to 2013–2014. The 2015–2016 cycle was used only to estimate direction priors (Section S1.5). Components were merged by the respondent identifier SEQN: demographics, depression screener, sleep, body measures, hospital utilisation, smoking, physical activity, medical conditions, diabetes and blood pressure questionnaires.
S1.3. Participants, outcome and sample size

We included respondents aged ≥ 18 years with valid responses (0–3) to all nine PHQ-9 items (DPQ010–DPQ090) [29]. Refused, don't-know and missing responses were not treated as symptom values; DPQ100 (functional difficulty) is not part of the total. With q_{ij} the response of participant i to item j,

All PHQ-9 items, the total score and any derived quantity were excluded from the predictors. Of 9,693 adults in 2017–March 2020, 1,385 had no depression screener record and 32 had at least one invalid item, leaving 8,276 participants (767 with PHQ-9 ≥ 10, 9.3%). Of 8,153 adults in 2021–2023, 2,634 had no screener record and 64 an invalid item, leaving 5,455 (723 positive, 13.3%). In 2005–2014, 4,082 of 30,295 adults had no screener record and 156 an invalid item, leaving 26,057 (2,294 positive, 8.8%) (Fig. 1 (main text)). Included and excluded participants are compared in Table S7. The development release was split 70/30 at participant level, stratified by outcome (seed 2026), into a development set (n = 5,793, 537 events) and an internal test set (n = 2,483).

All eligible participants were used. We checked the development set against the minimum sample size for a binary prediction model [30], assuming 25 predictor parameters, outcome prevalence 0.093 and an anticipated C statistic of 0.78, which corresponds to a Cox–Snell R² of 0.089. Shrinkage of at most 10% required 2,391 participants, a difference of at most 0.05 between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R² required 1,024, and estimating the overall risk within ±0.05 required 130. The largest, 2,391 participants with 222 events (8.9 events per parameter), is below the 5,793 participants and 537 events available (21.5 per parameter).
S1.4. Predictors and harmonisation

Candidate predictors had to be plausibly available before a symptom questionnaire, clearly defined, not derived from the outcome, and fielded with the same coding in 2017–2020 and 2021–2023. Fourteen variables qualified: age, sex, family income-to-poverty ratio, education (five levels), marital status (married/partnered, previously married, never married), body mass index, usual sleep duration on workdays and on free days, self-rated general health (five levels), current smoking, doctor-told diabetes, doctor-told hypertension, daily sedentary time, and a count of ten doctor-told chronic conditions (asthma, arthritis, congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina, myocardial infarction, stroke, liver condition, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cancer). All are survey items; self-rated health, sleep duration and sedentary time are interview questions, and the chronic conditions are self-reported 'doctor-told' answers rather than coded diagnoses (Table S14 marks which variables are usually held as structured record data).

Two predictors overlap in content with the PHQ-9. Sleep duration touches the sleep item but is asked in a separate questionnaire. Self-rated general health is the strongest predictor and plausibly reflects fatigue, sleep and appetite problems that the PHQ-9 asks about directly; a person who rates their health as poor may be reporting some of the same experience. Both are therefore closer to the outcome than demographic or record items, and we report models without them (Section S2.9). Contact with a mental health professional was not used, because it is close to the outcome. Race and ethnicity served only for subgroup evaluation. Two sleep items with strong associations in the earlier cycle (SLQ050, SLQ120) were not fielded in 2021–2023 and were examined only in a development-period sensitivity analysis. In the development set 20.0% of participants had at least one missing predictor, mostly income-to-poverty ratio (13.3%).

The 2005–2014 cycles required three harmonisation decisions, written into the analysis protocol (Section S1.12) before the files were downloaded: workday sleep came from SLD010H, recorded in whole hours; free-day sleep was not collected and was missing for every participant; and the chronic-condition count used the nine items available before the COPD item was introduced in 2013–2014. Sedentary time was not collected in 2005–2006. Marital status was mapped to the three categories above, and race and ethnicity before 2011 came from RIDRETH1, which has no separate Asian category. Variables absent in a cycle were left missing for every model.
S1.5. Base models

Abstention rules need a base model that produces a probability. We used three, chosen to separate the effect of the rule from that of the model: a fuzzy additive model whose terms are bounded, sign-constrained linear logistic regression, whose terms are unbounded, and logistic regression with restricted cubic splines, the best-ranking model in the later and earlier periods.

*Knowledge schema and fuzzy additive model.* A knowledge schema declares, for each of the 14 variables, its type, unit, NHANES source and admissible set (category sets for discrete variables, intervals for continuous ones; Table S14), together with 39 linguistic concepts (fuzzy sets [31]), the source of each cut-point and a direction prior. It is a typed, versioned declaration rather than an ontology with a reasoner [32], and it is released as a JSON-LD 1.1 file [33] in which concepts belong to one SKOS concept scheme [34]; the model code loads this file, so the released artefact is the one that produced the results (Fig. S5). Continuous variables are partitioned into trapezoidal concepts forming Ruspini partitions [35]. For break points b_1 < … < b_m, half-width h and admissible interval [l, u], the inner concepts have the trapezoidal membership

and the first and last concepts are shoulders that stay at 1 up to the range ends: μ_1(x) = min(1, max(0, (b_1 + h − x)/(2h))) and μ_{m+1}(x) = min(1, max(0, (x − b_m + h)/(2h))). Memberships of a variable's concepts therefore sum to one everywhere in [l, u], and every membership is constant beyond the outermost corners. Cut-points came from external conventions: WHO body-mass-index categories (18.5, 25, 30 kg/m²; h = 1) [36], the consensus recommendation of at least 7 h of sleep (short < 6.5 h, long > 9.5 h; h = 0.5) [37], 130% and 350% of the federal poverty level (h = 0.3), age bands at 35 and 60 years (h = 5) and sedentary-time bands at 4 and 8 h/day (h = 1). Ordinal and categorical variables have crisp set memberships (e.g. FairHealth, PoorHealth, Multimorbidity for ≥ 2 conditions).
A rule r has an antecedent A_r of one or two concepts and fires with strength μ_r(x) = min_{k ∈ A_r} μ_k(x_k). Rules combine additively on the log-odds scale,
η(x) = logit p(x) = β_0 + Σ_{r=1}^{R} β_r μ_r(x),   subject to s_r β_r ≥ 0,

a zero-order Takagi–Sugeno system [38] with log-odds consequents, where s_r ∈ {−1, 0, +1} is the direction prior of the rule's concepts. Priors were estimated in NHANES 2015–2016 (n = 5,134, 415 positive) as the sign of the risk ratio of PHQ-9 ≥ 10 for membership ≥ 0.5 versus < 0.5 when its 95% confidence interval excluded 1, and 0 otherwise (17 positive, 16 negative, 8 neutral; Table S4). Free-day sleep was not asked in 2015–2016, so its 3 concepts inherited the direction of the workday concepts; these priors were never estimated. The selected structure contains every single-concept rule except one reference concept per variable; two-concept rules could be added greedily, but 5-fold cross-validated AUROC in the development set (0.759, 0.756, 0.760, 0.754 and 0.759 for K = 0, 8, 16, 32, 64 added rules) selected none under the pre-specified parsimony rule (smallest K within 0.005 of the best). The model therefore has 25 single-concept rules and an intercept: a sign-constrained piecewise-linear additive model with knots at the schema's cut-points and constant tails. Coefficients were fitted by L-BFGS-B on the mean log-likelihood plus λ Σ_r β_r² (λ = 10⁻³), with the sign constraints as box bounds. For the point score a missing membership was replaced by its development-sample mean.

*Regression base models and other comparators.* Sign-constrained logistic regression used the raw inputs with median imputation, the direction priors imposed on main effects (age, BMI and sleep unconstrained because their associations are U-shaped) and a cross-validated L2 penalty (λ = 0.01). Logistic regression with restricted cubic splines [39] used four knots at the 5th, 35th, 65th and 95th development percentiles for age, BMI and both sleep durations, other inputs linear, and median imputation. Discrimination was also compared with logistic regression with missing-value indicators (the comparator named in the protocol), without indicators, and after multiple imputation by chained equations [40]; gradient-boosted trees [41, 42] with and without monotone constraints; and an explainable boosting machine (GA²M) [24, 26]. Version-level variants and single-element ablations of the fuzzy model (conjunctive version 1, 16 added pair rules, normalised TSK aggregation, no sign constraints, crisp memberships, quantile memberships without the schema, median imputation) are described in Section S4.
S1.6. Abstention rules

*Terminology.* A rule *decides* a person when it returns *refer* (recommend completing the PHQ-9 or an equivalent assessment) or *do not refer*; otherwise it *abstains*. *Coverage* is the proportion of participants decided. *Refer-on-abstain* is the policy that sends every abstention for assessment, so it turns any rule into a referral decision for everyone. *Selective prediction* is the general practice of deciding only when a model is confident enough, and abstaining otherwise [4].
Fig. 2 (main text) summarises the design: three base models, each held fixed while five abstention rules are applied to the same records under 16 missingness scenarios.

Every rule returns one of these three outputs for a person. Abstentions were never counted as negative predictions; we report decisions among decided participants and, as the conservative policy for prescreening, refer-on-abstain, in which every abstention is referred [3]. Each rule uses its base model's threshold t, fixed on development data (Section S1.11) and applied on the raw probability scale σ(η), before recalibration; for the fuzzy model t = 0.066. The rules differ in what they assume about the missing inputs.

*Worst-case bounds* assume nothing beyond the admissible set. Let O and M be the observed and missing variables of a person and 𝒳_M the product of the admissible sets of the missing variables. The rule computes
p_L = min σ(η(x_O, x_M)),   p_U = max σ(η(x_O, x_M)),   over x_M ∈ 𝒳_M,

and refers if p_L ≥ t, does not refer if p_U < t, and abstains otherwise. A decision that is made therefore holds for every admissible value of the missing inputs. The guarantee concerns the model's own output and the frozen threshold, not the outcome: if the model is miscalibrated in a population, as all models were in 2021–2023, a decision that holds for every completion can still be wrong, and it is wrong in the same way as the model's decision on a complete record. Section S1.7 describes how the bounds are computed for each base model.

*Imputation spread* uses the conditional distribution of the missing inputs given the observed ones, learnt in the development data. The imputation model is the one fitted for the chained-equation comparator: five chained-equation models (scikit-learn IterativeImputer with Bayesian ridge conditional models, posterior sampling and 10 iterations), fitted once on the development predictors and kept fixed for every cohort and scenario; they were never refitted on test data. Each conditional model regresses one input on all the others (the 14 predictors, with marital status as three indicators); the outcome was not included, because it is unknown when a prediction is made. The five models produced 20 completed copies of each record (four posterior draws from each; discrete inputs rounded and all inputs clipped to their admissible sets), the base model scored each copy, and the rule refers if at least 90% of the 20 probabilities exceed t, does not refer if at most 10% do, and abstains otherwise. Unlike the original analysis, in which the rule ran on the chained-equation logistic model, the imputations here pass through the same base model as the bounds, so the comparison holds the model fixed.

*Pattern submodels* [7] avoid assumptions about the missing values by not using them: for each missingness pattern in the evaluation data, the base model was refitted on the development set without the missing variables, with its own threshold chosen on out-of-fold predictions, and applied to the records with that pattern. Every record therefore receives a decision. Because the number of patterns grows quickly when many inputs are masked at random, pattern submodels were evaluated under natural, non-random, outcome-dependent and shifted missingness, where patterns are few, but not under 30% MCAR. *Complete-case abstention* decides only records with every input observed. *Point-score selective prediction* ignores which inputs are missing: the base model's point score (single imputation as in Section S1.5) is compared with the threshold, and the rule abstains when the score lies within a band around the threshold, |logit p − logit t| < δ. The half-width δ was set on development out-of-fold predictions so that 90% of development participants would be decided. This is ordinary selective classification [4] with no missing-data rule, and it shows what the other rules add to it.

We did not use conformal prediction as a baseline. For a binary outcome, split-conformal prediction with a score-based nonconformity measure returns the set {0, 1}, the analogue of abstention, whenever the predicted probability falls in a band set by the target coverage level [43]; it is then a point-score rule like the one above, and the band does not depend on which inputs are missing. Conformal methods designed for missing inputs calibrate the band within missingness patterns and guarantee coverage of the label set marginally or conditionally on the pattern, under exchangeability between calibration and test data [8]. That guarantee concerns a different quantity from ours (how often the true label lies in the set, rather than whether the decision depends on the missing values), and it is lost under the period shift and non-random missingness studied here. Work on imputation for prediction shows that, with enough data, imputation followed by a flexible model can be consistent even when values are not missing at random [9]; imputation spread is the abstention counterpart of that approach.
S1.7. Computing worst-case bounds

Because σ is monotone it suffices to bound η. For the regression base models the bound is direct: in sign-constrained linear regression each missing input moves η linearly, so its extremes lie at the ends of the admissible interval (or at one of the three marital categories); in spline regression each missing input was optimised separately over a 2,001-point grid. For the fuzzy additive model the bounds depend on the rule structure.

*Main-effects rule bases (Algorithm 1).* When every rule involves one variable, η is a sum of univariate functions g_v(x_v) = Σ_{r on v} β_r μ_r(x_v), so its extremes over 𝒳_M are the sums of each missing variable's extremes. Each g_v is continuous and piecewise linear with breakpoints at the trapezoid corners of Eq. (2), and constant beyond the outermost corners, so its extremes on [l, u] lie in the finite set of range ends and corners inside the range (Box 1 (main text)). The constant tails also mean that the width of the bound does not grow with the admissible range once the range covers the outermost corners, whereas a linear term, or a spline with linear tails, gives a bound that grows with the range. The point score, the development-mean imputation of each membership, always lies in [p_L, p_U] for a main-effects model, because η is linear in the memberships and the mean membership vector is a convex combination of admissible vectors.

*Rule bases with conjunctions (Algorithm 2).* The conjunctive version 1 of the system, retained as a comparator, and the variant with 16 added pair rules contain two-concept rules min(μ_k(x_k), μ_m(x_m)), which couple variables. Missing variables are grouped into connected components (two missing variables are connected if a rule contains both); η is a constant plus a sum of functions of the components, so its extremes are sums of per-component extremes. For each component, Algorithm 2 (Box 2 (main text)) enumerates the categories of its discrete variables and, for each combination, a finite candidate set for its continuous variables. The candidate sets are exact by the following two statements.

*Statement 1 (one continuous missing variable).* Let x ∈ [l, u] be the only continuous missing variable of a component, with its discrete variables fixed. Then g(x) = Σ_r β_r min(μ_{k(r)}(x), c_r), where c_r ∈ [0, 1] is the observed partner membership of rule r (c_r = 1 for single-concept rules). Each μ_k is continuous and piecewise linear with breakpoints at its trapezoid corners, and min(μ_k(x), c_r) adds breakpoints only where μ_k(x) = c_r, i.e. at x = a + c_r(b − a) and x = d − c_r(d − c). Hence g is continuous and piecewise linear on [l, u] with breakpoints in the finite set 𝒞 = {l, u} ∪ {corners} ∪ {solutions of μ_k(x) = c_r}. A continuous piecewise-linear function on a closed interval attains its extremes at an endpoint or a breakpoint, so enumerating 𝒞 is exact. □

*Statement 2 (two continuous missing variables).* Let (x, z) ∈ [l_x, u_x] × [l_z, u_z] be connected through pair rules min(μ_k(x), μ_m(z)). Partition each axis at its breakpoints from Statement 1. On each resulting rectangle every membership is affine, so each pair term equals one of two affine functions, switching along the line μ_k(x) = μ_m(z). These lines cut the rectangle into convex polygons on which η is affine; η is continuous, so its extremes over the rectangle lie at polygon vertices. Every vertex is a rectangle corner, an intersection of a switching line with a rectangle edge, or an intersection of two switching lines inside the rectangle, and enumerating these points on all rectangles is exact. □

Components with more than two continuous missing variables fall back to the box bound obtained by letting each missing membership range over [0, 1]; this is a valid outer bound, not an exact one, and the trace flags it. For a component with m_c categorical combinations, n_b breakpoints per axis and q pair rules, the cost is O(m_c n_b) evaluations for one continuous variable and O(m_c n_b² q²) for two. Algorithm 2 was checked against a 41-point grid augmented with trapezoid corners and against dense brute force (Section S2.7).
S1.8. Missingness scenarios

*Natural missingness.* All models were applied to the three validation cohorts as observed. In 2005–2014 free-day sleep was not collected and sedentary time was not collected in 2005–2006; income-to-poverty ratio is missing for 7.5–13.3% of participants in every cohort.

*Choice of simulated scenarios.* The simulated scenarios were chosen to violate, one at a time, the assumption each rule relies on, not to reproduce a particular survey. MCAR is the setting in which imputation is valid and pattern submodels are impractical. Non-random masking of income and of self-rated health mimics the item non-response seen in surveys, where people with low income or poor health answer less often, at a moderate and at an extreme strength. Outcome-dependent masking is the hardest case for imputation, because the missing value carries information about the outcome that the observed inputs do not. Structural absence with a shifted conditional distribution is the case for which worst-case bounds were proposed. Real missingness is likely to be milder than the extreme scenarios and to mix mechanisms, so the scenarios bracket rather than represent practice.

*Simulated missingness on the internal test set* (10 repetitions each, the same masks for every model and rule): (i) MCAR, each of the 12 predictors other than age and sex masked with probability 0.3 (other rates and the removal of whole domains are in Section S4); (ii) MNAR, income-to-poverty ratio masked with probability 0.6 if below 1.3 and 0.1 otherwise, self-rated health masked with probability 0.6 if fair or poor and 0.1 otherwise, or both; (iii) stronger MNAR, the same selections with probabilities 0.9 and 0.05; (iv) outcome-dependent masking, self-rated health and income-to-poverty ratio each masked with probability 0.6 in participants with PHQ-9 ≥ 10 and 0.1 otherwise.

*Structural absence with a shifted conditional distribution.* Imputation spread draws a missing input from its conditional distribution given the observed inputs in the development data. To test the rules where that distribution is wrong for the target population, we removed one input for everyone, as free-day sleep was removed in 2005–2014, in target samples whose relation between that input and the other inputs departs from the development data. For self-rated health and for free-day sleep in turn, a linear model fitted on development data predicted the input from the other 13, and each internal test participant received the standardised residual z_i of their observed value. A target sample of the same size was drawn with replacement with probabilities proportional to exp(γ s z_i), where s = +1 for self-rated health (worse health than predicted) and s = −1 for free-day sleep (shorter sleep than predicted), and γ = 0, 0.5 or 1 (10 samples each). With γ = 1 the mean residual in the target sample was +0.94 SD for self-rated health and −1.23 SD for free-day sleep, so an imputation model trained on development data systematically imputes healthier values and longer sleep than the truth. The input was then masked for every participant. Because the outcome is related to both inputs, the resampling also changed the prevalence of PHQ-9 ≥ 10 in the target samples; we report it for each sample, and we compare rules on sensitivity as well as on counts per 1,000. The residual of self-rated health, a five-level ordinal variable, came from a linear model because it serves only to tilt the sampling weights towards participants whose health is worse than their other inputs predict. To check that this choice does not drive the results, the γ = 1 shift for self-rated health was repeated with the probability-scale residual of a proportional-odds model, P(Y < y) − P(Y > y) [44].
S1.9. Comparison of abstention rules

Rules were compared with the base model held fixed, on four kinds of output. (1) Coverage, the proportion of participants decided, split into decisions to refer and decisions not to refer. (2) Classification of decided participants at matched coverage: each rule ranks participants by its confidence (distance of the bounds from the threshold on the log-odds scale; distance of the imputation share from 0.5; for pattern submodels, point-score selective prediction and complete cases, distance of the score from the threshold) and decides the most confident ones up to the coverage reached by worst-case bounds of the same base model; we report sensitivity, specificity and balanced accuracy among them. (3) The risk–coverage curve [4], balanced error among the decided against the proportion decided over coverage 0.05–1, summarised by the area under it (AURC; lower is better) with a percentile bootstrap interval (500 resamples of participants in the natural cohorts, 300 in 2005–2014 and in the first repetition of each simulated scenario) and a paired interval for the difference to worst-case bounds. (4) Decision consequences under refer-on-abstain, per 1,000 participants: participants referred, cases missed and questionnaires avoided (participants not referred), and net benefit [45] at threshold probabilities 0.05 and 0.10, with paired percentile bootstrap intervals for the difference to worst-case bounds (1,000 resamples; 500 in 2005–2014; first repetition of the simulated scenarios). Differences whose interval includes zero are described as equivalent. Balanced accuracy at matched coverage depends on which participants each rule chooses to decide, so the decision-consequence measures are the ones that correspond to the prescreening costs of Section S1.1.
S1.10. Bound-guided input acquisition

An abstention means that at least one missing input could change the decision. The acquisition rule (Algorithm 3, Box S1) asks for one missing input at a time: for each candidate v it estimates the probability ρ_{v} that observing v alone resolves the decision, evaluating the bounds at support points of the development-set distribution of v (all categories, or 25 quantile points for continuous inputs) with the other missing inputs still unknown, requests the input with the largest ρ_{v}, and stops when the decision is resolved or no requestable input remains. A cost-weighted variant requests the input with the largest ρ_{v}/c_{v}. We compared it with a fixed order by each input's contribution range, a cost order that requests structured record items first (diabetes, hypertension, chronic conditions, BMI, smoking, marital status, education), then income, then interview items, and a random order, on internal test records with 10% or 30% of inputs masked at random and later-period records with 30% masked. A requested masked input was revealed with its true value; inputs missing in the original data could not be requested, so in 2005–2014 free-day sleep can never be requested and acquisition was not evaluated there. Policies were compared on the number of inputs and on expected item cost per abstention, with illustrative costs of 1 for a record item, 2 for income and 3 (or 5) for an interview item. Differences are paired by record (2,000 bootstrap resamples). Every order resolves the same records with the same final decisions.

x: S1.11. Performance measures and statistical analysis

Every model produced out-of-fold predictions in the development set by 5-fold cross-validation. These were used to fit a Platt recalibration map and to fix the referral threshold as the largest raw score reaching an out-of-fold sensitivity of at least 0.80. Models were then refitted on the whole development set and applied unchanged to all cohorts. We report AUROC, AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, proportion flagged, Brier score, calibration slope and observed-to-expected ratio (O/E) [46], and net benefit across threshold probabilities 0.02–0.30 [45, 47]. Confidence intervals came from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of participants (500 for AUROC in single cycles); AUROC differences used 2,000 paired resamples with percentile intervals and two-sided bootstrap p-values, which are not reported for differences smaller than 0.001. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals; intervals for differences, which may include negative values, are written 'a to b', and other intervals 'a–b'. Proportions are given to one decimal, AUROC, AURC and balanced accuracy to three and net benefit to four. Because NHANES has a stratified cluster design, the primary comparison was repeated with a design-based bootstrap that resamples primary sampling units within strata (75 strata, 154 units in 2005–2014). AUROC weighted by interview weights is a sensitivity analysis. To include training variability, the fuzzy model, its variants and five comparators were refitted on 100 repeated stratified 70/30 splits of the 2017–2020 release with hyperparameters fixed; we report the mean and SD of each AUROC difference. Recalibration-in-the-large was examined by estimating an intercept shift on a random half of the 2021–2023 or 2005–2014 cohort and evaluating it on the other half (200 repetitions). Subgroup AUROC, sensitivity and O/E were computed by sex, age band and race and ethnicity where at least 10 positive cases were available; because sensitivity differed by sex, we also examined sex-specific thresholds (target sensitivity ≥ 0.80 in each sex) and sex-specific recalibration-in-the-large.

The PHQ-2 reference used items DPQ010 and DPQ020 with the usual cut-point ≥ 3 [20, 21]. These two items are part of the nine summed in the reference standard, so their accuracy against PHQ-9 ≥ 10 is inflated by incorporation bias; against diagnostic interviews, PHQ-2 ≥ 3 had a pooled sensitivity of 0.72 and specificity of 0.85 in an individual participant data meta-analysis [21], which is the fairer reference. A record-typical model used only age, sex, BMI, diabetes, hypertension, chronic-condition count, smoking, education and marital status.
S1.12. Development history, protocol and post hoc analyses

The fuzzy model above is the second version of the system. Version 1 selected K = 32 rules of any arity by a greedy procedure with no forced main effects; 30 of its 32 rules were two-concept conjunctions. On the internal and later-period sets it trailed logistic regression by 0.023 (−0.0429 to −0.0033) and 0.012 (−0.0246 to −0.0002) AUROC. We attributed the gap to the absence of main effects, tested that diagnosis with development-set cross-validation only, and wrote a protocol that fixed the revised structure, the K grid and selection rule, the comparators (logistic regression with missing indicators and gradient-boosted trees) and ablations, the 2005–2014 cohorts and their harmonisation, and the primary comparison: AUROC in 2005–2014 of the fuzzy model versus logistic regression with missing indicators. According to the protocol's addendum, the 2005–2014 files were downloaded after the protocol was saved; no independently verifiable record predates the download, and the earliest verifiable record of the protocol is its deposit with the code (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23827787); the protocol file is unchanged in every later release. The 2005–2014 comparison is therefore free of earlier results according to our records only. We therefore classify the analyses in three groups. The primary analysis is that pre-specified comparison. Secondary analyses were also pre-specified: the other performance measures, the comparators and ablations named in the protocol, worst-case coverage and MCAR masking. Exploratory analyses were specified after the original results were known: every other comparator, every abstention rule other than worst-case bounds, every simulated scenario other than MCAR, the acquisition rule, the repeated splits and the design-based analysis. Tables mark exploratory analyses with ‡; their results should be read as hypothesis-generating, although the comparison of abstention rules, the main subject of the paper, falls in this group.
S1.13. Explanation trace, software and use of generative AI

For each person the system exports a JSON trace with the inputs, missing-input flags, each concept's membership and provenance, each rule's contribution β_r μ_r (or its range when an input is missing), the intercept, the probability bounds and, for abstentions, the input requested by Algorithm 3. For complete inputs the contributions add exactly to η, as in any generalised linear model.

Analyses used Python 3.13 with pandas 3.0.5, scikit-learn 1.9.1, SciPy 1.18.1, statsmodels and interpret 0.7.8. The analysis code was drafted with a generative AI tool (Claude, Anthropic) under the authors' specification: cohort construction, models, bounds, the acquisition rule, experiments, figure scripts and the three verification tests. The authors specified what each test checks; the test files were implemented with the same tool, so they are independent of the analysis code in construction, not in authorship. tests/test_bounds_bruteforce.py compares the bounds with dense brute-force evaluation of the model on 4,001-point grids and shares no code with Algorithms 1 and 2; tests/test_trace_fidelity.py recomputes probabilities from serialised traces without importing the model; tests/test_cohort_priors.py reproduces the cohort flow and the direction priors from the public files. The tool was also used to help structure the manuscript and edit its language. The authors reviewed the code, outputs and text and checked references and statistics against their sources. All analyses use the seed 2026. The release that accompanied the previous version of this manuscript was re-run from the raw files in a clean directory and reproduced every number except computing times; the analyses added since then were run once with the archived code. All numbers are written by the analysis code to one statistics file and inserted programmatically.
S2. Extended results
S2.1. Cohorts

Table 1 (main text) summarises the cohorts. Prevalence of PHQ-9 ≥ 10 was 8.8% in 2005–2014, 9.3% in 2017–2020 and 13.3% in 2021–2023. The 2021–2023 cohort was older and more educated, with fewer participants rating their health as fair or poor but more sedentary time and more chronic conditions. The 2005–2014 cohort was younger, had more current smokers and reported about half an hour less workday sleep, partly because sleep was recorded in whole hours. Every 2005–2014 participant lacked free-day sleep; excluding that input, 30.2% had at least one missing predictor, against 18.3% in the internal test set and 18.0% in 2021–2023. Excluded adults of the development release were slightly older and more often women than included adults (Table S7).
S2.2. Knowledge schema and rule base

Direction priors from 2015–2016 agreed with established epidemiology: low income (RR 2.44 (2.01–2.96)), current smoking (2.69 (2.24–3.24)), poor self-rated health (5.39 (4.43–6.56)), multimorbidity (2.33 (1.93–2.82)), short (1.28 (1.04–1.58)) and long (1.89 (1.51–2.35)) workday sleep were positive; college education (0.44 (0.33–0.58)) and being married or partnered (0.51 (0.42–0.61)) were negative. Of the 25 rules, 20 carry a sign constraint; none of the constrained coefficients sits at its zero bound, and refitting without constraints changed no sign, so the constraints were not binding. Table S15 lists the rules. Each coefficient is a contrast with the reference concept of its variable; the negative coefficients of NormalWeight and Overweight, for example, are contrasts with Obese. One coefficient shapes the 2005–2014 bounds: within free-day sleep the reference concept contributes 0, ShortSleepFreeDay +0.433 and LongSleepFreeDay +0.038, so with free-day sleep unknown the lower bound adds nothing and the upper bound adds up to 0.433 log-odds. The sign constraint on ShortSleepFreeDay comes from an inherited prior that was never estimated. The point score instead adds 0.068 log-odds, the development-mean memberships of the two concepts weighted by their coefficients, to every 2005–2014 participant.
S2.3. Base models: discrimination and calibration

The pre-specified primary comparison was AUROC in 2005–2014: 0.787 (0.778–0.797) for the fuzzy model against 0.779 for logistic regression with missing indicators, a difference of +0.008 (+0.0031 to +0.0135; design-based interval +0.0046 to +0.0119). This contrast is uninformative about the fuzzy model or its schema. Free-day sleep was not collected in 2005–2014; the indicator model applies a learnt indicator coefficient to everyone and over-predicts (O/E 0.74), whereas logistic regression without indicators reached 0.787, the same as the fuzzy model (−2.2 × 10⁻⁵, −0.0048 to +0.0049; design-based −0.0037 to +0.0036). Refitted without free-day sleep, the fuzzy model reached 0.789 and regression without indicators 0.792. Spline regression ranked best in the later and earlier periods (0.763 and 0.797; difference to the fuzzy model in 2005–2014 −0.010, design-based −0.0134 to −0.0064). Internally the fuzzy model was the lowest of the main models (0.780 against 0.786–0.794). Over 100 repeated splits of 2017–2020 it averaged 0.764 (SD 0.013), and its mean difference to linear logistic regression was −0.006 (SD 0.008). Design-based intervals were close to participant-level intervals and changed no conclusion (Table S1; Fig. S1). The base models therefore discriminated about equally well, and none should be read as superior for prediction. Differences of 0.01 AUROC are small in operational terms: with each model's threshold set to reach 80% sensitivity in 2005–2014, the fuzzy model flagged 430 participants per 1,000, regression without indicators 426 and spline regression 407, so the better-ranking spline model would save about 23 referrals per 1,000 at the same sensitivity. The differences that matter for this study are those between abstention rules, not between base models.

x: S2.4. Abstention rules with the base model held fixed

Throughout this section, a decision made by worst-case bounds is one that holds for every admissible value of the missing inputs *under the model*. It is not a guarantee that the decision is correct: where the model is miscalibrated, as all models were in 2021–2023, a decision that holds for every completion can still be wrong.

*Cohorts as observed.* Where few inputs were missing (internal test and 2021–2023), the five rules differed little: with the fuzzy model, worst-case bounds decided 95.1% of internal test participants, imputation spread 97.9%, point-score selective prediction 90.9% and complete cases 81.4%, balanced accuracy at matched coverage ranged from 0.705 to 0.709, and every AURC interval for the difference to worst-case bounds included zero (Table 2 (main text)). In 2005–2014, where free-day sleep was missing for everyone, the rules separated. With the fuzzy model, worst-case bounds decided 69.2% of participants (41.6% referred, 27.6% not referred), imputation spread 83.3% (43.3% and 40.0%), point-score selective prediction 89.9%, pattern submodels everyone and complete cases nobody; weighted by interview weights, worst-case coverage was 69.5% and imputation-spread coverage 83.9%. The asymmetry of the worst-case decisions follows from the free-day sleep coefficients (Section S2.2): with the upper bound raised by up to 0.433 log-odds, 'do not refer' required a low risk from every other input. Among decided participants, worst-case bounds had sensitivity 93.8% and specificity 43.9%, against 88.5% and 51.9% for imputation spread on the same model. At the coverage of worst-case bounds, balanced accuracy was 0.689 for worst-case bounds, 0.710 for imputation spread, 0.721 for pattern submodels and 0.726 for point-score selective prediction, and AURC was 0.338, 0.303, 0.295 and 0.289 (Fig. 3 (main text)). Ranking participants by the distance of the fuzzy model's point score from the threshold thus gave the lowest AURC in 2005–2014, lower than pattern submodels by −0.006 (−0.007 to −0.005); with sign-constrained regression the two did not differ (−0.001 to +0.001), and with spline regression the point score was again better (−0.018 to −0.016). The same ordering of worst-case bounds against the other rules held with the regression base models, by a wider margin for spline regression, whose linear tails widen the bounds: worst-case coverage 52.2% and balanced accuracy 0.708, against 85.4% and 0.775 for imputation spread.

*Random and non-random missingness.* Under 30% MCAR, worst-case bounds decided 33.5% of participants, imputation spread 66.0% and point-score selective prediction 88.6% with the fuzzy model; at matched coverage balanced accuracy was 0.641, 0.716 and 0.732, and the regression models showed the same gap (Table S16). Non-random missingness of income changed little. Non-random missingness of self-rated health, the strongest predictor, narrowed the differences. With masking probabilities 0.9 in fair or poor health and 0.05 otherwise, worst-case bounds decided 85.1%, imputation spread 91.3% and pattern submodels everyone; balanced accuracy at matched coverage was 0.712, 0.718 and 0.706; and the fuzzy model's AURC was lowest for worst-case bounds (0.238, SD 0.003 over repetitions, against 0.257 and 0.254). With the regression base models the rules were within 0.01 AURC of each other. Under outcome-dependent masking, worst-case bounds had a slightly lower AURC than imputation spread and pattern submodels for every base model, by at most 0.016 (SD over repetitions 0.003–0.005 for the fuzzy model), with first-repetition intervals that included zero.

*Structural absence with a shifted conditional distribution.* When self-rated health was absent for everyone, worst-case bounds of the fuzzy model decided 40.7% of participants without shift and 43.3% with γ = 1, and with γ = 1 those of sign-constrained and spline regression 4.9% and 5.8%, because the full range of self-rated health spans most of the linear predictor. The shift also raised the prevalence of PHQ-9 ≥ 10 in the target samples, from 9.3% (γ = 0) to 12.1% and 14.2% (Table S16). Measured by sensitivity under refer-on-abstain, the shift degraded imputation and pattern submodels modestly: from 90.7% to 87.4% for imputation spread and from 80.4% to 75.3% for pattern submodels, against 99.3% and 98.6% for worst-case bounds; most of the rise in cases missed per 1,000 (from 8.7 to 17.9 for imputation spread) reflects the larger number of cases. At matched coverage the decided records were still classified better by imputation spread (0.686 against 0.536), pattern submodels (0.720) and point-score selective prediction (0.719). Repeating the γ = 1 shift with ordinal residuals, which correlated 0.99 with the linear residuals, gave the same picture (prevalence 13.9%; balanced accuracy 0.541, 0.691 and 0.721; sensitivity 98.8%, 88.9% and 78.1%). With free-day sleep absent and shifted, the ordering of 2005–2014 was reproduced (balanced accuracy 0.668, 0.695, 0.703 and 0.712).
S2.5. Summary across scenarios

Table 3 (main text) condenses the 16 scenarios for the fuzzy model, and separates results that held across scenarios from those confined to a few. Three results held in every scenario with substantial missingness. Worst-case bounds decided the fewest participants, missed the fewest cases and avoided the fewest questionnaires; their net benefit at 0.10 was never above that of the best other rule; and when an input was absent for everyone, pattern submodels or point-score selective prediction did best on both AURC and net benefit (worst-case AURC up to 0.138 higher). Two results were confined to particular mechanisms. Worst-case bounds had the lowest AURC in 7 of the 16 scenarios, all with non-random or outcome-dependent masking or in 2021–2023, but by at most 0.010. With intervals that pool all repetitions of the simulated scenarios, their net benefit at 0.10 was lower than that of the best rule in 8 scenarios and equivalent in 8; it was not higher in any.

S3.1. Relation to other approaches and what the schema contributes

Worst-case bounds are the credal-classifier logic [5, 6] applied to an additive model with declared admissible sets, and imputation spread is the abstention counterpart of impute-then-predict, which can be consistent even when values are not missing at random if the predictor is flexible enough [9]. Pattern submodels [7] did well here because the patterns were few; with many sporadic patterns they need sharing of information across patterns. Conformal prediction with missing values [8] guarantees the coverage of label sets within patterns under exchangeability; its abstentions depend on the score band rather than on which inputs are missing, and the guarantee is lost under the period shift studied here, which is why we did not use it as a baseline. Risk–coverage evaluation comes from selective classification [4].

The knowledge schema did not improve ranking: the fitted model is a sign-constrained piecewise-linear additive model whose constraints were not binding, and removing the schema left discrimination within noise. What the schema contributes is the admissible set of each input, which worst-case bounds need and a fitted model does not carry, and auditability: each of the 25 terms is a named concept with a declared cut-point source and prior in a machine-readable file that the code loads, in line with interpretability criteria for fuzzy systems [48]. The audit also exposes the declarations' limits, such as the prior for free-day sleep that was inherited rather than estimated and that sets the width of the 2005–2014 bounds. The sign priors mattered only for the conjunctive version 1, where they pruned incoherent conjunctions; there, univariable and mutually adjusted priors gave similar discrimination (0.777 and 0.772 in 2005–2014), so we draw no conclusion about which kind of prior is better.
S3.2. Transport across survey periods

All models under-predicted in 2021–2023 by a similar factor, and a single intercept shift repaired it. NHANES documentation records several changes after the pandemic suspension that plausibly contributed: the depression screener moved from an interviewer-administered computer-assisted interview to audio computer-assisted self-interview [49], a mode change known to increase reporting of sensitive symptoms [50]; oversampling by race, Hispanic origin and income was discontinued [51]; and unweighted interview and examination response rates fell to 34.5% and 25.6% from 51.0% and 46.9% in 2017–March 2020 [52, 53]. We cannot separate these from a real rise in prevalence [54, 55], but the self-administration change alone is reason to expect a model trained on interviewer-administered data to under-predict. Any deployment would require local recalibration and monitoring regardless of model type or abstention rule [46].
S3.3. Limitations

The fuzzy model was designed after version-1 results on the internal and later-period sets had been seen, and the protocol that fixed it was not registered; that it preceded the download of the 2005–2014 files rests on our records only. The abstention-rule comparisons, including every scenario that could have reversed the ordering, were specified after the original results were known. Both validation cohorts are periods of the same survey. The simulated scenarios are stylised: the shift was induced by resampling one test set, and the masking probabilities were chosen to be strong rather than estimated. Pattern submodels were not evaluated under many sporadic patterns. Imputation spread used one chained-equation model with 20 draws and a 90/10 rule; other imputation models or cut-offs could change coverage. All estimates are unweighted, and only the primary comparison has a design-based interval. The outcome is a questionnaire threshold, not a diagnostic interview [11], and self-rated health, the strongest predictor, overlaps in content with it. The acquisition rule was evaluated only under random masking with true values revealed, its support points come from the marginal development distribution of each input, and its item costs are illustrative. Conformal abstention, credal classifiers for non-additive models and learned acquisition policies [57] were discussed but not fitted. Subgroup analyses were descriptive and underpowered for several groups.
